addedLines: - agent-sdk-dev:agent-sdk-verifier-py: Use this agent to verify that a Python Agent SDK application is properly configured, follows SDK best practices and documentation recommendations, and is ready for deployment or testing. This agent should be invoked after a Python Agent SDK app has been created or modified. (Tools: All tools)

- agent-sdk-dev:agent-sdk-verifier-ts: Use this agent to verify that a TypeScript Agent SDK application is properly configured, follows SDK best practices and documentation recommendations, and is ready for deployment or testing. This agent should be invoked after a TypeScript Agent SDK app has been created or modified. (Tools: All tools)
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- feature-dev:code-architect: Designs feature architectures by analyzing existing codebase patterns and conventions, then providing comprehensive implementation blueprints with specific files to create/modify, component designs, data flows, and build sequences (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- feature-dev:code-explorer: Deeply analyzes existing codebase features by tracing execution paths, mapping architecture layers, understanding patterns and abstractions, and documenting dependencies to inform new development (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- feature-dev:code-reviewer: Reviews code for bugs, logic errors, security vulnerabilities, code quality issues, and adherence to project conventions, using confidence-based filtering to report only high-priority issues that truly matter (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- plugin-dev:agent-creator: Use this agent when the user asks to "create an agent", "generate an agent", "build a new agent", "make me an agent that...", or describes agent functionality they need. Trigger when user wants to create autonomous agents for plugins. Examples:

<example>
Context: User wants to create a code review agent
user: "Create an agent that reviews code for quality issues"
assistant: "I'll use the agent-creator agent to generate the agent configuration."
<commentary>
User requesting new agent creation, trigger agent-creator to generate it.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User describes needed functionality
user: "I need an agent that generates unit tests for my code"
assistant: "I'll use the agent-creator agent to create a test generation agent."
<commentary>
User describes agent need, trigger agent-creator to build it.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User wants to add agent to plugin
user: "Add an agent to my plugin that validates configurations"
assistant: "I'll use the agent-creator agent to generate a configuration validator agent."
<commentary>
Plugin development with agent addition, trigger agent-creator.
</commentary>
</example> (Tools: Write, Read)

- plugin-dev:plugin-validator: Use this agent when the user asks to "validate my plugin", "check plugin structure", "verify plugin is correct", "validate plugin.json", "check plugin files", or mentions plugin validation. Also trigger proactively after user creates or modifies plugin components. Examples:

<example>
Context: User finished creating a new plugin
user: "I've created my first plugin with commands and hooks"
assistant: "Great! Let me validate the plugin structure."
<commentary>
Plugin created, proactively validate to catch issues early.
</commentary>
assistant: "I'll use the plugin-validator agent to check the plugin."
</example>

<example>
Context: User explicitly requests validation
user: "Validate my plugin before I publish it"
assistant: "I'll use the plugin-validator agent to perform comprehensive validation."
<commentary>
Explicit validation request triggers the agent.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User modified plugin.json
user: "I've updated the plugin manifest"
assistant: "Let me validate the changes."
<commentary>
Manifest modified, validate to ensure correctness.
</commentary>
assistant: "I'll use the plugin-validator agent to check the manifest."
</example> (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- plugin-dev:skill-reviewer: Use this agent when the user has created or modified a skill and needs quality review, asks to "review my skill", "check skill quality", "improve skill description", or wants to ensure skill follows best practices. Trigger proactively after skill creation. Examples:

<example>
Context: User just created a new skill
user: "I've created a PDF processing skill"
assistant: "Great! Let me review the skill quality."
<commentary>
Skill created, proactively trigger skill-reviewer to ensure it follows best practices.
</commentary>
assistant: "I'll use the skill-reviewer agent to review the skill."
</example>

<example>
Context: User requests skill review
user: "Review my skill and tell me how to improve it"
assistant: "I'll use the skill-reviewer agent to analyze the skill quality."
<commentary>
Explicit skill review request triggers the agent.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User modified skill description
user: "I updated the skill description, does it look good?"
assistant: "I'll use the skill-reviewer agent to review the changes."
<commentary>
Skill description modified, review for triggering effectiveness.
</commentary>
</example> (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-simplifier: Use this agent when code has been written or modified and needs to be simplified for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. This agent should be triggered automatically after completing a coding task or writing a logical chunk of code. It simplifies code by following project best practices while retaining all functionality. The agent focuses only on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise.

Examples:

<example>
Context: The assistant has just implemented a new feature that adds user authentication to an API endpoint.
user: "Please add authentication to the /api/users endpoint"
assistant: "I've implemented the authentication for the /api/users endpoint. Here's the code:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
Since a logical chunk of code has been written (authentication feature), use the Task tool to launch the code-simplifier agent to improve the code's clarity and maintainability while preserving functionality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now let me use the code-simplifier agent to refine this implementation for better clarity and maintainability"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just fixed a bug by adding several conditional checks.
user: "Fix the null pointer exception in the data processor"
assistant: "I've added the necessary null checks to prevent the exception:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After modifying code to fix a bug, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the fix follows best practices and maintains code quality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Let me refine this bug fix using the code-simplifier agent to ensure it follows our best practices"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just refactored a function to improve performance.
user: "Optimize the data sorting algorithm for better performance"
assistant: "I've optimized the sorting algorithm. Here's the updated implementation:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After completing a performance optimization task, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and maintainable.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now I'll use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and follows our coding standards"
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:pr-test-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to review a pull request for test coverage quality and completeness. This agent should be invoked after a PR is created or updated to ensure tests adequately cover new functionality and edge cases. Typical triggers include the user asking whether tests on a freshly-created PR are thorough, an updated PR adding new logic that needs coverage analysis, and a final pre-merge double-check before marking a PR ready. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:

<example>
Context: Daisy has just finished implementing a new feature that fetches data from an API with fallback behavior.
Daisy: "I've added error handling to the API client. Can you review it?"
Assistant: "Let me use the silent-failure-hunter agent to thoroughly examine the error handling in your changes."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has created a PR with changes that include try-catch blocks.
Daisy: "Please review PR #1234"
Assistant: "I'll use the silent-failure-hunter agent to check for any silent failures or inadequate error handling in this PR."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has just refactored error handling code.
Daisy: "I've updated the error handling in the authentication module"
Assistant: "Let me proactively use the silent-failure-hunter agent to ensure the error handling changes don't introduce silent failures."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:type-design-analyzer: Use this agent when you need expert analysis of type design in your codebase. Specifically use it (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, and (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- vercel:ai-architect: Specializes in architecting AI-powered applications on Vercel — choosing between AI SDK patterns, configuring providers, building agents, setting up durable workflows, and integrating MCP servers. Use when designing AI features, building chatbots, or creating agentic applications. (Tools: All tools)

- vercel:deployment-expert: Specializes in Vercel deployment strategies, CI/CD pipelines, preview URLs, production promotions, rollbacks, environment variables, and domain configuration. Use when troubleshooting deployments, setting up CI/CD, or optimizing the deploy pipeline. (Tools: All tools)

- vercel:performance-optimizer: Specializes in optimizing Vercel application performance — Core Web Vitals, rendering strategies, caching, image optimization, font loading, edge computing, and bundle size. Use when investigating slow pages, improving Lighthouse scores, or optimizing loading performance. (Tools: All tools)

- playwright-skill: Complete browser automation with Playwright. Auto-detects dev servers, writes clean test scripts to /tmp. Test pages, fill forms, take screenshots, check responsive design, validate UX, test login flows, check links, automate any browser task. Use when user wants to test websites, automate browser interactions, validate web functionality, or perform any browser-based testing.
- audit-tier: Identify the protection tier, owner, and import blast radius of a file or directory under overrides/. Use before editing anything you're unsure about.
- code-quality: Audit recently changed or specified files for code quality issues — naming, circular imports, TypeScript coverage, test/story existence, and structural debt. Read-only. Use after implementing a feature or before opening a PR.
- code-review: AI-powered code review using CodeRabbit. Default code-review skill. Trigger for any explicit review request AND autonomously when the agent thinks a review is needed (code/PR/quality/security).
- contentful-register-component: Register a Zimmermann React component with Contentful Studio Experiences. Use when a developer asks to register, add, or expose a React component to Contentful, or when they need to create a Contentful component definition for an existing component.
- feature-spec: Turn a plain-English feature request into a scoped implementation plan before any code is written. Asks one clarifying question at a time, then produces a spec Claude Code can execute safely. Use this before starting any non-trivial implementation session.
- generate-changelog: Generate a release changelog from conventional commits and upstream baseline notes. Produces audience-specific outputs for the dev team, QA, product, and GitHub Release. Use before cutting a release branch or when preparing release notes.
- new-component: Scaffold a new Zimmermann component under overrides/app/components/ — TypeScript, Chakra-first, with a paired Storybook story. Use whenever a new custom component is needed.
- onboarding: Interactive onboarding for new developers and QA engineers joining the Zimmermann PWA Kit project. Asks role at the start, checks the mechanical setup items, then orients the person to the rules and tools relevant to their role and squad. Run this in the first Claude Code session on a new machine or a first day on the project.
- pr-checklist: Generate a PR description and merge checklist based on the files changed on the current branch. Pairs with /code-quality.
- project-init: One-time project setup walkthrough. Runs the state detection script, fixes automatable items, asks one question at a time for human-input items, and updates the 7.1c CI/CD & Environment Setup Checklist Confluence page as each item is confirmed. Run this once when setting up the project for the first time, or when returning to check setup status.
- qa-generate: Generate a Gherkin .feature file and Playwright test spec from a Jira story. Human-in-the-lead — Lead QA validates the .feature before Playwright is generated. Use for any new storefront user journey that needs E2E test coverage.
- scope-check: Review a proposed Claude Code prompt for scope safety before it runs. Classifies every likely-touched file by tier and verdicts the prompt SAFE / RISKY / BLOCKED, rewriting it when needed.
- session-start: Run the mandatory session start ritual — reads tracking docs, runs branch + health checks, states current position. Use at the start of every coding session.
- upstream-sync-review: Review the release notes / changelog for a new @salesforce/retail-react-app version before bumping. Lightweight policy — see .docs/upstreamPolicy.md.
- code-review:code-review: Code review a pull request
- feature-dev:feature-dev: Guided feature development with codebase understanding and architecture focus
- ralph-loop:cancel-ralph: Cancel active Ralph Loop
- ralph-loop:help: Explain Ralph Loop plugin and available commands
- ralph-loop:ralph-loop: Start Ralph Loop in current session
- commit-commands:clean_gone: Cleans up all git branches marked as [gone] (branches that have been deleted on the remote but still exist locally), including removing associated worktrees.
- commit-commands:commit-push-pr: Commit, push, and open a PR
- commit-commands:commit: Create a git commit
- claude-md-management:revise-claude-md: Update CLAUDE.md with learnings from this session
- pr-review-toolkit:review-pr: Comprehensive PR review using specialized agents
- agent-sdk-dev:new-sdk-app: Create and setup a new Claude Agent SDK application
- plugin-dev:create-plugin: Guided end-to-end plugin creation workflow with component design, implementation, and validation
- vercel:bootstrap: Bootstrap a repository with Vercel-linked resources by running preflight checks, provisioning integrations, verifying env keys, and then executing db/dev startup commands safely.
- vercel:deploy: Deploy the current project to Vercel. Pass "prod" or "production" as argument to deploy to production. Default is preview deployment.
- vercel:env: Manage Vercel environment variables. Commands include list, pull, add, remove, and diff. Use to sync environment variables between Vercel and your local development environment.
- vercel:status: Show the status of the current Vercel project — recent deployments, linked project info, and environment overview.
- frontend-design:frontend-design: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
- superpowers:brainstorming: You MUST use this before any creative work - creating features, building components, adding functionality, or modifying behavior. Explores user intent, requirements and design before implementation.
- superpowers:dispatching-parallel-agents: Use when facing 2+ independent tasks that can be worked on without shared state or sequential dependencies
- superpowers:executing-plans: Use when you have a written implementation plan to execute in a separate session with review checkpoints
- superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch: Use when implementation is complete, all tests pass, and you need to decide how to integrate the work
- superpowers:receiving-code-review: Use when receiving code review feedback, before implementing suggestions, especially if feedback seems unclear or technically questionable - requires technical rigor and verification, not performative agreement or blind implementation
- superpowers:requesting-code-review: Use when completing tasks, implementing major features, or before merging to verify work meets requirements
- superpowers:subagent-driven-development: Use when executing implementation plans with independent tasks in the current session
- superpowers:systematic-debugging: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes
- superpowers:test-driven-development: Use when implementing any feature or bugfix, before writing implementation code
- superpowers:using-git-worktrees: Use when starting feature work that needs isolation from current workspace or before executing implementation plans - ensures an isolated workspace exists via native tools or git worktree fallback
- superpowers:using-superpowers: Use when starting any conversation - establishes how to find and use skills, requiring skill invocation before ANY response including clarifying questions
- superpowers:verification-before-completion: Use when about to claim work is complete, fixed, or passing, before committing or creating PRs - requires running verification commands and confirming output before making any success claims; evidence before assertions always
- superpowers:writing-plans: Use when you have a spec or requirements for a multi-step task, before touching code
- superpowers:writing-skills: Use when creating new skills, editing existing skills, or verifying skills work before deployment
- claude-md-management:claude-md-improver: Audit and improve CLAUDE.md files in repositories. Use when user asks to check, audit, update, improve, or fix CLAUDE.md files. Scans for all CLAUDE.md files, evaluates quality against templates, outputs quality report, then makes targeted updates. Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- figma:figma-code-connect: Creates and maintains Figma Code Connect template files that map Figma components to code snippets. Use when the user mentions Code Connect, Figma component mapping, design-to-code translation, or asks to create/update .figma.ts or .figma.js files.
- figma:figma-create-new-file: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE every `create_new_file` tool call. NEVER call `create_new_file` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user wants a new blank Figma file — a new design, FigJam, or Slides file — or when you need a fresh file before calling `use_figma`. Usage — /figma-create-new-file [editorType] [fileName] (e.g. /figma-create-new-file figjam My Whiteboard, /figma-create-new-file slides Q3 Review)
- figma:figma-design-to-code: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE calling the `get_design_context` Figma MCP tool. You MUST trigger this skill whenever the user wants to implement, build, port, or code up a Figma design as code. Example prompts (not exhaustive) are 'implement this Figma design', 'build this screen from Figma', 'turn this Figma into code', 'design to code'. This skill provides critical instructions and steps to the agent on how to correctly implement Figma designs in code and must NOT be skipped.
- figma:figma-generate-design: Use this skill alongside figma-use when the task involves translating an application page, view, or multi-section layout into Figma. Triggers: 'write to Figma', 'create in Figma from code', 'push page to Figma', 'take this app/page and build it in Figma', 'create a screen', 'build a landing page in Figma', 'update the Figma screen to match code', 'convert this modal/dialog/drawer/panel to Figma'. This is the preferred workflow skill whenever the user wants to build or update a full page, modal, dialog, drawer, sidebar, panel, or any composed multi-section view in Figma from code or a description. Discovers design system components, variables, and styles from Code Connect files, existing screens, and library search, then imports them and assembles views incrementally section-by-section using design system tokens instead of hardcoded values.
- figma:figma-generate-diagram: MANDATORY prerequisite — load this skill BEFORE every `generate_diagram` tool call. NEVER call `generate_diagram` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user asks to create, generate, draw, render, sketch, or build a diagram — flowchart, architecture diagram, sequence diagram, ERD or entity-relationship diagram, state diagram or state machine, gantt chart, or timeline. Also trigger when the user mentions Mermaid syntax or wants a system architecture, decision tree, dependency graph, API call flow, auth handshake, schema, or pipeline visualized in FigJam. Routes to type-specific guidance, sets universal Mermaid constraints, and tells you when to use a different diagram type or skip the tool entirely (mindmaps, pie charts, class diagrams, etc.).
- figma:figma-generate-library: Build or update a professional-grade design system in Figma from a codebase. Use when the user wants to create variables/tokens, build component libraries, create individual components with proper variant sets and variable bindings, set up theming (light/dark modes), document foundations, or reconcile gaps between code and Figma. Also use when the user asks to create or generate any component in Figma — even a single one — since components require proper variable foundations, variant states, and design token bindings to be production-quality. This skill teaches WHAT to build and in WHAT ORDER — it complements the `figma-use` skill which teaches HOW to call the Plugin API. Both skills should be loaded together.
- figma:figma-implement-motion: Translates Figma motion and animations into production-ready application code. Use when implementing animation/motion from a Figma design — user mentions "implement this motion", "add animation from Figma", "animate this component", provides a Figma URL whose node is animated, or when `get_design_context` returns motion data or instructs you to call `get_motion_context`.
- figma:figma-swiftui: SwiftUI ↔ Figma translation. Use whenever the user mentions Swift, SwiftUI, iOS, iPhone, or iPad — in EITHER direction — translating a Figma design into SwiftUI (design → code), or pushing SwiftUI views / screens / tokens back into a Figma file (code → design). Triggers on phrases like 'implement this Figma design in SwiftUI', 'build this screen in Swift', 'push this SwiftUI view to Figma', 'mirror my Swift code in a Figma file', or whenever a Figma URL appears alongside `.swift` files / an `.xcodeproj`. Routes to a direction-specific reference doc; loads alongside `figma-use` for the code → design path.
- figma:figma-use: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE every `use_figma` tool call. NEVER call `use_figma` directly without loading this skill first. Skipping it causes common, hard-to-debug failures. Trigger whenever the user wants to perform a write action or a unique read action that requires JavaScript execution in the Figma file context — e.g. create/edit/delete nodes, set up variables or tokens, build components and variants, modify auto-layout or fills, bind variables to properties, or inspect file structure programmatically.
- figma:figma-use-figjam: This skill helps agents use Figma's use_figma MCP tool in the FigJam context. Can be used alongside figma-use which has foundational context for using the use_figma tool.
- figma:figma-use-motion: Motion / animation context for the `use_figma` MCP tool — animating Figma nodes via manual keyframes, animation styles, easing, and timeline duration. Load alongside figma-use whenever a task involves adding, editing, or inspecting animation on a node.
- figma:figma-use-slides: This skill helps agents use Figma's use_figma MCP tool in the Slides context. Can be used alongside figma-use which has foundational context for using the use_figma tool.
- claude-code-setup:claude-automation-recommender: Analyze a codebase and recommend Claude Code automations (hooks, subagents, skills, plugins, MCP servers). Use when user asks for automation recommendations, wants to optimize their Claude Code setup, mentions improving Claude Code workflows, asks how to first set up Claude Code for a project, or wants to know what Claude Code features they should use.
- plugin-dev:agent-development: This skill should be used when the user asks to "create an agent", "add an agent", "write a subagent", "agent frontmatter", "when to use description", "agent examples", "agent tools", "agent colors", "autonomous agent", or needs guidance on agent structure, system prompts, triggering conditions, or agent development best practices for Claude Code plugins.
- plugin-dev:command-development: This skill should be used when the user asks to "create a slash command", "add a command", "write a custom command", "define command arguments", "use command frontmatter", "organize commands", "create command with file references", "interactive command", "use AskUserQuestion in command", or needs guidance on slash command structure, YAML frontmatter fields, dynamic arguments, bash execution in commands, user interaction patterns, or command development best practices for Claude Code.

{"baseRefName":"develop","body":"## Summary

- New workflow `sync-env-vars-to-mrt.yml` — triggered manually from GitHub Actions → Run workflow
- No hardcoded variable names: reads `.env.sample` for the key list, fetches actual values from the selected GitHub Environment via the GitHub API, then intersects the two
- Only keys that are **set and non-empty** in the GitHub Environment are PATCHed to MRT — missing keys are silently skipped so MRT retains existing values
- `scope:personal` and `scope:auto` keys (including `ENVIRONMENT_NAME`) are never synced
- Supports **dry run** mode — shows exactly what would be synced without touching MRT

## How it works

```
.env.sample  →  parse scope:shared + scope:tier keys
                        ↓
GitHub API   →  GET /environments/{target}/variables  (all set vars)
                        ↓
intersection →  keys in both + non-empty value
                        ↓
MRT API      →  PATCH /projects/zimmermann/target/{target}/env-var/
```

## Usage

**GitHub Actions → Workflows → "Sync Env Vars to MRT" → Run workflow**

Select target (`dev` / `test` / `sit` / `uat` / `staging` / `prod`) and optionally enable dry run.

## Test plan

- [ ] Run with `dry_run: true` for `dev` — verify output lists the expected keys without calling MRT
- [ ] Run with `dry_run: false` for `dev` — verify MRT target shows updated values in Runtime Admin
- [ ] Add a new key to `.env.sample` — verify it appears in the next sync without any workflow change
- [ ] Leave a key unset in the GitHub Environment — verify it is skipped in the sync log

<details>
<summary>🧩 Analysis chain</summary>

🌐 Web query:

`Can the default GITHUB_TOKEN read repository environment variables via the GitHub REST API, and what permission scope is required?`

💡 Result:

Yes, the default GITHUB_TOKEN can be used to read repository variables via the GitHub REST API, provided it has been granted the necessary permissions [1]. To read these variables, you must explicitly configure the permissions scope in your GitHub Actions workflow file using the permissions key [2][3]. Specifically, you need to grant the variables permission [1]. To do this, add the following configuration to your workflow or job: permissions: variables: read If you also need to modify (create or update) these variables, you would set the permission to write: permissions: variables: write Without explicitly granting these permissions, the GITHUB_TOKEN will typically return a 404 Not Found or a Resource not accessible by integration error when attempting to interact with repository variables, as the default permissions for the GITHUB_TOKEN are often restricted [1]. Note that these permissions apply to the variables defined in your repository or environment settings, which are distinct from the environment variables managed via the env key in your workflow YAML file [1][4].

Citations:

- 1: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/77273776/in-github-actions-how-do-i-modify-an-env-variable-in-the-repository-settings-f
- 2: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/tutorials/authenticate-with-github_token
- 3: https://docs.github.com/actions/reference/authentication-in-a-workflow
- 4: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-what-workflows-do/use-variables

🌐 Web query:

`GitHub Actions environment variables REST API GITHUB_TOKEN permission scope read repository environment variables`

💡 Result:

The default GITHUB_TOKEN provided in GitHub Actions workflows cannot be used to read or modify repository environment variables via the GitHub REST API [1][2][3]. Attempts to use the GITHUB_TOKEN for these endpoints typically result in a "403 Resource not accessible by integration" error or similar authorization failures, as these operations require higher administrative privileges than the GITHUB_TOKEN possesses [3]. To interact with repository environment variables via the REST API, you must use an alternative authentication method with appropriate permissions [1][3]: 1. Fine-Grained Personal Access Token (PAT): You can create a PAT with the necessary "Variables" permission (set to read and write) and "Metadata" permission (set to read-only) [2]. If the repository is private, ensure the token also has the required repository access [1][2]. If you are part of an organization, the PAT may require approval by an organization owner [2]. 2. content.content:
name: Sync Env Vars to MRT

# Reads all keys tagged `mrt:true` in .env.sample, fetches their values from
# the selected GitHub Environment via the GitHub API, then PATCHes only the
# keys that are actually set (non-empty) to the MRT target.
#
# Keys that exist in .env.sample but have no value in the GitHub Environment
# are silently skipped — MRT retains whatever value it already holds for them.
#
# CI/tooling vars (CODERABBIT_API_KEY, JIRA_URL, BROWSERSTACK_*, E2E_* etc.)
# are not tagged mrt:true and are never included in the sync.
#
# scope:personal and scope:auto keys (including ENVIRONMENT_NAME) are never
# synced — they are developer-local or script-injected.
#
# ⚠️  PRODUCTION is intentionally excluded from this workflow.
#     Production MRT env vars must be updated manually in the MRT console
#     (runtime.commercecloud.com) by a tier-1-approver. This ensures prod
#     changes go through a human gate rather than an automated workflow.
#
# Trigger: manual only (workflow_dispatch). Run after updating a GitHub
# Environment to propagate new values to MRT without a full redeploy.

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      target:
        description: 'MRT target to update (prod excluded — update manually in MRT console)'
        required: true
        type: choice
        options:
          - dev
          - test
          - sit
          - uat
          - staging
      dry_run:
        description: 'Dry run — show what would be synced without calling MRT'
        required: false
        type: boolean
        default: false

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  sync:
    name: Sync to MRT (${{ inputs.target }})
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: ${{ inputs.target }}
    env:
      MRT_USER: ${{ secrets.MRT_USER }}
      MRT_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.MRT_API_KEY }}
      MRT_PROJECT: zimmermann
      GH_REPO: ${{ github.repository }}

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'

      - name: Parse syncable keys from .env.sample
        id: parse
        run: |
          python3 - <<'PYEOF'
          import re, os, json

          # Only keys explicitly tagged `# mrt:true` in .env.sample are synced.
          # CI/tooling vars (CODERABBIT_API_KEY, JIRA_URL, BROWSERSTACK_*, E2E_* etc.)
          # are intentionally not tagged and are excluded from MRT.
          keys = []
          pending_mrt = False
          with open('.env.sample') as f:
              for line in f:
                  line = line.rstrip('\n')
                  if re.match(r'^#\s*mrt:true', line):
                      pending_mrt = True
                      continue
                  stripped = line.strip()
                  if not stripped or stripped.startswith('#'):
                      if not stripped:
                          pending_mrt = False
                      continue
                  eq = stripped.find('=')
                  if eq == -1:
                      pending_mrt = False
                      continue
                  key = stripped[:eq].strip()
                  if pending_mrt:
                      keys.append(key)
                  pending_mrt = False

          print(f'Parsed {len(keys)} MRT-tagged keys from .env.sample')
          with open(os.environ['GITHUB_OUTPUT'], 'a') as out:
              out.write(f'keys={json.dumps(keys)}\n')
          PYEOF

      - name: Fetch GitHub Environment variables
        id: gh_vars
        run: |
          python3 - <<'PYEOF'
          import json, os, subprocess, sys

          TARGET = os.environ['TARGET']
          REPO   = os.environ['GH_REPO']

          # GitHub Environment variables are readable via the API (plain-text by design —
          # see .env.sample header note). --paginate returns all pages in one call.
          all_vars = {}
          result = subprocess.run(
              ['gh', 'api', f'/repos/{REPO}/environments/{TARGET}/variables',
               '--paginate', '--jq', '.variables[] | {(.name): .value}'],
              capture_output=True, text=True
          )
          if result.returncode != 0:
              print(f'GitHub API error: {result.stderr}', file=sys.stderr)
              sys.exit(1)
          # gh --jq outputs one JSON object per line when iterating
          for line in result.stdout.strip().splitlines():
              if line:
                  all_vars.update(json.loads(line))

          print(f'Found {len(all_vars)} variables set in GitHub Environment: {TARGET}')
          with open(os.environ['GITHUB_OUTPUT'], 'a') as out:
              out.write(f'vars={json.dumps(all_vars)}\n')
          PYEOF
        env:
          TARGET: ${{ inputs.target }}
          # Fine-grained PAT with Environments: read access to this repo only
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GH_ENV_READ_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build payload and sync to MRT
        run: |
          python3 - <<'PYEOF'
          import base64, json, os, sys, urllib.request, urllib.error

          DRY_RUN = os.environ.get('DRY_RUN', 'false').lower() == 'true'
          TARGET  = os.environ['TARGET']
          PROJECT = os.environ['MRT_PROJECT']
          USER    = os.environ['MRT_USER']
          API_KEY = os.environ['MRT_API_KEY']

          syncable_keys = json.loads(os.environ['SYNC_KEYS'])
          gh_vars       = json.loads(os.environ['GH_VARS'])

          # Intersect: only keys in .env.sample that have a value in GitHub
          payload = {}
          skipped_empty = []
          skipped_missing = []
          for key in syncable_keys:
              if key in gh_vars:
                  val = gh_vars[key]
                  if val:
                      payload[key] = val
                  else:
                      skipped_empty.append(key)
              else:
                  skipped_missing.append(key)

          print(f'Keys to sync:    {len(payload)}')
          print(f'Skipped (empty): {len(skipped_empty)}')
          print(f'Skipped (not in GitHub Environment): {len(skipped_missing)}')
          if skipped_missing:
              print('  Not set:', ', '.join(skipped_missing[:20]),
                    '...' if len(skipped_missing) > 20 else '')

          if not payload:
              print('Nothing to sync.')
              sys.exit(0)

          if DRY_RUN:
              print(f'\nDRY RUN — would PATCH {len(payload)} keys to MRT target: {TARGET}')
              for k in sorted(payload):
                  print(f'  {k}')
              sys.exit(0)

          token = base64.b64encode(f'{USER}:{API_KEY}'.encode()).decode()
          url   = f'https://cloud.mobify.com/api/projects/{PROJECT}/target/{TARGET}/env-var/'
          req   = urllib.request.Request(
              url,
              data=json.dumps(payload).encode(),
              method='PATCH',
              headers={
                  'Authorization': f'Basic {token}',
                  'Content-Type': 'application/json',
              },
          )
          try:
              resp = urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30)
              print(f'\nMRT response: {resp.status} {resp.reason}')
              print(f'Synced {len(payload)} env vars to MRT target: {TARGET}')
          except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
              print(f'MRT API error {e.code}: {e.read().decode()}', file=sys.stderr)
              sys.exit(1)
          except urllib.error.URLError as e:
              print(f'MRT API connection error: {e.reason}', file=sys.stderr)
              sys.exit(1)
          except TimeoutError:
              print('MRT API request timed out after 30 s', file=sys.stderr)
              sys.exit(1)
          PYEOF
        env:
          TARGET: ${{ inputs.target }}
          DRY_RUN: ${{ inputs.dry_run }}
          SYNC_KEYS: ${{ steps.parse.outputs.keys }}
          GH_VARS: ${{ steps.gh_vars.outputs.vars }}

# active line below is preceded by its own `# scope:shared`, `# scope:tier`,
# `# scope:personal`, or `# scope:auto` comment line (parsed by
# scripts/switchEnv.mjs, ignored by everything else — kept on its own line,
# not trailing on the KEY=value line, so a blank placeholder here still reads
# as genuinely empty to the pre-commit secret guard):
#   scope:shared   — same value across all 6 tiers (dev/test/sit/uat/staging/prod)

#                    in `push`/`init`'s pull to/from GitHub Environments.
#   scope:tier     — differs per tier. Lives in the gitignored .env.<tier> for
#                    whichever tier you're pointing local dev at; also
#                    included in `push`/pull.

#                    (your own Atlassian token, your own Contentful CMA token)
#                    that must never be centralized — still lives in
#                    .env.shared, but `push`/`init`'s pull skip it entirely.
#                    Each developer fills this in themselves.
#   scope:auto     — never hand-set; scripts/switchEnv.mjs injects this itself.

# Managed Runtime environment (storefront runtime config). Only keys tagged
# `mrt:true` are synced by the "Sync Env Vars to MRT" GitHub Actions workflow.
# CI/tooling vars (CODERABBIT_API_KEY, JIRA_URL, BROWSERSTACK_*, E2E_* etc.)

| -------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `npm run build`                  | Dev                           | Production build (local verification)                                  |
| `npm run analyze-build`          | Dev                           | Production build with the webpack bundle analyzer                       |
| `npm run save-credentials`       | Dev — one-time setup          | One-time MRT auth — required before any `push`                          |
| `npm run push`                   | Integration/SI Partner ⚠️     | Build + push to the currently active `DEPLOY_TARGET` — a shared environment |
| `npm run push:<tier>`             | Integration/SI Partner ⚠️     | Build + push to a specific tier — already automated on merge via CI; manual runs deploy to a shared environment |

#### Syncing env vars to MRT

GitHub Actions → **Sync Env Vars to MRT** → Run workflow.

Reads all `scope:shared` and `scope:tier` keys from `.env.sample`, fetches their values from the selected GitHub Environment, and PATCHes only the keys that are set (non-empty) to the corresponding MRT target. Keys missing from the GitHub Environment are silently skipped — MRT retains whatever value it already holds.

| Input    | Values                                     | Notes                                               |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `target` | `dev` / `test` / `sit` / `uat` / `staging` | MRT target to update                               |
| `dry_run`| `true` / `false` (default)                | Print keys that would be synced without calling MRT |

> **Production is intentionally excluded from this workflow.** Update production MRT env vars manually in the [MRT console](https://runtime.commercecloud.com) → Environments → `prod` → Environment Variables. This ensures prod changes go through a human gate (tier-1-approver) rather than an automated workflow.

Only keys tagged `# mrt:true` in `.env.sample` are synced — CI/tooling vars (`CODERABBIT_API_KEY`, `JIRA_URL`, `BROWSERSTACK_*`, `E2E_*` etc.) are not tagged and are never pushed to MRT.

**Required repository secrets** — set once under GitHub → Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → Repository secrets:

| Secret | How to obtain | Notes |
| ------ | ------------- | ----- |
| `MRT_USER` | [runtime.commercecloud.com](https://runtime.commercecloud.com) → Account → API credentials | Your MRT account username (email) |
| `MRT_API_KEY` | Same page → generate or copy API key | Scoped to the `zimmermann` project |
| `GH_ENV_READ_TOKEN` | GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens → Generate new token | Set **Repository access** to this repo only; grant **Environments: Read** permission. Use a service account token where possible — personal tokens rotate with the person. Do not use a classic PAT (`repo` scope is too broad). |

Run this workflow after updating a GitHub Environment to propagate new values to MRT without triggering a full redeploy.

## Choice Input Validation

A choice input renders as a dropdown populated with options you define directly in the YAML, and GitHub validates that the submitted value is one of the listed options - no free text is accepted via the UI.

## UI vs. API/CLI Behavior

The validation appears to be **UI-specific**. GitHub validates that the submitted value is one of the listed options through the UI, but the search results suggest that when using the GitHub API or CLI, you may be able to pass arbitrary string values since the validation is enforced at the UI layer.

content.text:
I reviewed PR #42 (`feat(ci): sync GitHub Environment vars to MRT on demand`) against your own CHANGES_REQUESTED review from 2026-07-27 — you're the requested reviewer (confirmed via `gh api user`), so this is verifying mani060689's fixes before you re-approve.

**Your two Must-Fix items — both resolved, verified against the actual diff:**

1. **Ungated prod path** — `prod` is fully removed from the workflow's `target` choice list (`.github/workflows/sync-env-vars-to-mrt.yml`), not just gated. README and an in-file comment now say prod must be updated manually via the MRT console by a tier-1-approver. This is a cleaner fix than the environment-protection-rule approach you suggested — no automated path to prod exists at all now, rather than a rule that could later be removed/misconfigured.
2. **CI secrets leaking into MRT** — resolved via a new `# mrt:true` tag in `.env.sample`. I checked the actual file: `CODERABBIT_API_KEY`, `JIRA_*`, `CONFLUENCE_*`, `BROWSERSTACK_*`, `E2E_*`, `RETAIL_APP_HOME` are all correctly *un*tagged; genuine runtime vars (Commerce, Contentful, Adyen, Global-e, etc.) are correctly tagged. I also checked that `scripts/switchEnv.mjs` (untouched by this PR) still parses fine — its scope-tag regex just skips any comment line it doesn't recognize, so the new `mrt:true` line doesn't break `npm run env`.

**Should-fix items — both resolved correctly:**
- Fine-grained PAT: README now points to a fine-grained `GH_ENV_READ_TOKEN` (Environments: read only), and it's scoped to just the fetch step's `env:`, not the whole job.
- `URLError` handling: added alongside the existing `TimeoutError` handler — and both are actually needed, not redundant: Python's `urlopen` wraps a connect-phase timeout in `URLError`, but a read-phase timeout surfaces as a bare `TimeoutError`. Keeping both covers both cases correctly.

**One thing I verified further, worth a quick decision:** GitHub's `workflow_dispatch` `type: choice` restriction is generally understood to be enforced by the UI dropdown, but not necessarily by the REST API/`gh workflow run` (i.e., someone could still dispatch with `-f target=prod` as a raw string). I couldn't fully confirm this either way. However, I checked and **the `prod` GitHub Environment currently has zero secrets configured** — so even in that bypass scenario, the job would hit `MRT_USER`/`MRT_API_KEY` as empty and fail before touching anything. So there's no live exploit path today, just a theoretical one if someone adds prod secrets to that environment later without revisiting this. A one-line runtime guard (reject if `$TARGET` isn't in an explicit allow-list) would close it permanently for near-zero cost, but I wouldn't call it a blocker given the current state.

Scope check: only `.env.sample`, the workflow file, and `README.md` changed — matches the PR description, no surprise touches to other Tier 1/2 files.

**My recommendation: this is in good shape to approve as-is.** Want me to post the approval on GitHub (I'm authenticated as your `marcelannavarro` account), or would you rather request the extra defense-in-depth guard first, or handle the approval yourself?

The storefront reads published content via the **Delivery API (CDA)** from both SSR and the browser, reads draft content via the **Preview API (CPA)** in editor sessions, and receives **publish webhooks** to clear the SSR cache.

66:- **SSR first.** Editorial content for SEO- and LCP-critical pages (homepage, PLP, PDP, campaign landings) is fetched server-side. The browser hydrates from the SSR payload — no CDA call on first paint.
67-- **GraphQL for composed pages.** Where a page assembles many entries the storefront uses the GraphQL Content API to fetch only the needed fields in one request. REST CDA is used for simpler reads.
68:- **Live preview.** When an editor opens preview in Contentful Studio, the storefront renders inside Studio's iframe. It detects the preview origin, switches to the CPA-backed MRT proxy, and refreshes on `postMessage` events from Studio.
69-- **Asset delivery.** Images come from `images.ctfassets.net`. The storefront generates `srcset`, `sizes`, AVIF with WebP fallback, and quality parameters per breakpoint.

74-|---|---|---|
75-| Delivery API token (CDA) | Browser bundle and SSR | Public — read-only, scoped to one environment. Safe to embed. |
76:| Preview API token (CPA) | MRT preview proxy only | Semi-sensitive — exposes drafts. MRT environment variable. Never reaches the browser. |
77-| Management API token (CMA) | Build-time schema sync script | High. Held on the CI host only. Never embedded. |
78-| Webhook shared secret | MRT webhook receiver | High. Verifies HMAC on inbound publish webhooks. MRT environment variable. |

85-|---|---|---|

87-| Contentful → Storefront | JSON entries with resolved linked references | CDA / Preview API response |
88-| Contentful → Storefront (assets) | Image and video asset URLs | Images API |
--
124:- The CPA token is held server-side only and is never logged.
125-- The CMA token is held only on the CI host — never embedded, never in PR diffs.
126-- No PII is handled by Contentful.

129-
130-1. **`regions` content-model field.** The working assumption is that region-specific entries are filtered by a `regions` field containing the relevant SFCC site IDs. Pending content-strategy and editor-workflow sign-off — this field affects how editors author content across all eight storefronts.
131-2. **SFCC vs Contentful content ownership on composed pages.** The principle is settled — SFCC owns all commerce data, Contentful owns editorial. Not yet confirmed is the split on composed pages: which editorial blocks appear on PDP and PLP, whether they are authored in SFCC Page Designer or Contentful, whether category landing pages are SFCC-routed or built in Contentful Studio Experiences, and whether the mega-menu includes Contentful-authored promotional tiles. The working assumption is in the ownership table in §1.
132:3. **Contentful Space and per-environment credentials.** Contentful to provide per-environment CDA token, CPA token, Space ID, environment ID, and webhook secret so the storefront can be tested against a real Contentful environment.

A correction to what I told you earlier: I'd only read the review-level reply comment at that point, and concluded nothing was fixed. That was wrong — there's a real fix commit I'd missed. Here's the accurate picture.

**Corrected timeline (all times UTC, converted from the commit's recorded +10:00):**

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 07-27 07:26:13 | You file CHANGES_REQUESTED: 2 must-fix, 4 should-fix, 1 non-blocking |
| 07-28 **04:28:04** | mani060689 pushes commit `9d0cd8c` — a real fix commit, co-authored with Claude Sonnet 4.6 |
| 07-28 04:28:45 | mani060689 posts a review-reply, 41s later — explaining what they did and didn't change |
| 07-28 05:21:21 | mani060689 comments `@coderabbitai review` — no-ops, since CodeRabbit already auto-reviewed `9d0cd8c` on push |
| 07-28 05:23:34 | PR closed, ~2 min later, no closing comment |

**What `9d0cd8c` actually fixed** (verified against the real diff):
- ✅ Rules-of-Hooks violation — extracted `ExperienceFetch` child component so `useFetchBySlug` is called unconditionally
- ✅ Race condition — added the `active`/stale-request guard in `contentfulPreview`'s `useEffect`
- ✅ `console.log` — removed
- ✅ Normal `/:slug` traffic leaking drafts — now correctly uses the delivery token/host unless `isPreview` is explicitly true
- ✅ `.mcp.json` — reverted the `b2c-dx-mcp` addition entirely (simpler than your "pin a version" suggestion — just dropped it, presumably for a separate PR)
- 🟡 Duplicated client logic — **partially** addressed: shared *constants* (`CONTENTFUL_FALLBACK_LOCALE`, host strings, preview origin) moved to `config/contentful.ts`, but each page still has its own separate `useMemo`/`createClient` call — you asked for one shared hook; that didn't happen.

**What's still genuinely open** (I checked the current code directly, not just CodeRabbit's markers):
- ❌ **Must-Fix #1's core point** — the `/preview` route still builds a Contentful client in the browser with `previewAccessToken` and calls `preview.contentful.com` directly. I checked `.docs/integration/02-contentful.md` §3/4/9 myself: it unambiguously states the CPA token is "held server-side in MRT; never reaches the browser... requests proxied through an MRT preview endpoint," and separately that it must "never be logged" and is exposed only via "MRT environment variable." The code contradicts that as clearly as you said. mani060689's reply asserts this is intentional (needed for the Live Preview SDK's postMessage mechanism) but doesn't update the doc or add the gate you asked for — they made a unilateral call on the exact question you posed as "yours to make together," rather than closing the loop on it.
- ❌ **Must-Fix #2** — I grepped the full PR branch for `noindex`/`robots`: zero matches. The `/preview` route in `routes.tsx` is registered exactly as before — unconditional, all environments, `exact: true`, no gating, no meta tag. This wasn't touched at all, and wasn't even mentioned in mani060689's reply.

**Bottom line:** this wasn't "closed with nothing done" — 5 of 7 items got real fixes, one commit, genuinely helped by Claude Code. But the two things that made your review a *hard* block — the doc-contradiction on where the CPA token lives, and the ungated/crawlable prod route — were left open, and the PR was closed within two minutes of a no-op CodeRabbit ping rather than either continuing to iterate or replying to explain why closing (vs. fixing or reopening the doc conversation) was the right call.

Want me to draft a comment for the closed PR laying this out (must-fix #1 and #2 still open, here's what's fixed) so there's a clear record before you decide whether to ask mani060689 to reopen, or take it over yourself?

content.text:
Re-reading the reply text closely, you're right that it does gesture at both — I undersold that in my last message. Let me break down precisely what was said and check each claim against the actual repo state, rather than take it at face value.

**What the reply actually said, mapped to your two Must-Fix items:**

- **Must-Fix #1 (token in browser)** — directly addressed for both sub-cases: `/preview` is "intentional" (SDK needs it for postMessage), `?preview` on `/:slug` is conceded as valid but deferred ("outside scope of this sprint," with a follow-up noted).
- **Must-Fix #2 (ungated + not noindex)** — never addressed by name, but the `/preview` argument ("not linked from any storefront navigation... it's not a public-facing page") is doing double duty as an implicit rebuttal to it too.

**Checking the "not a public-facing page" claim against the actual repo:**

- `robots.txt` on this branch: `User-agent: *` / `Disallow:` (empty) — crawling is **fully permitted, site-wide**. There's no robots-level block on `/preview` backing up the "not public" claim.
- Neither `contentfulPreview/index.tsx` nor `experience/index.tsx` renders any Seo/Helmet/meta component at all — confirmed by grep, zero hits.
- The base template's own `Seo` component (`node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/components/seo`) **already has a working `noIndex` prop** (`<meta name="robots" content="noindex">`) — it's not built yet as an override here, but using it would've been a ~1-line addition, not new infrastructure.

So "not linked from nav" is true, but it's not the same claim as "can't be discovered or indexed" — no internal link doesn't stop a crawler that finds the URL any other way (an external backlink, a Contentful editor pasting the preview link somewhere public, log/referrer exposure, or just guessing `/preview?entry=<id>`), and once found, nothing here stops it being indexed. Noindex exists precisely for "unlinked but guessable" pages — that's the standard mitigation, and it was available essentially for free. **This part of the reasoning doesn't hold up**, and it's not just a judgment call they made differently — a trivially cheap, already-existing mechanism went unused with no reason given at all.

There's also a sharper risk than "duplicate content in search results" here: since the CPA token isn't scoped to one entry, anyone who loads `/preview` gets a space-wide Preview API token in their own browser's network tab, extractable and reusable directly against Contentful's API to browse *every* draft entry in the space — not just the one they were linked to.

**On the `?preview` deferral** — "outside scope of this sprint" is a defensible engineering call on its own, but it doesn't satisfy this project's own process for a must-fix item: AGENTS.md requires stopping and getting explicit sign-off when a doc conflict is punted, not just asserting it in a comment and closing the PR. Your review explicitly framed this as a decision for the two of you to land on together (update the doc, or build the proxy) — deferring is a legitimate third option, but it needed your agreement, which was never actually sought before closing.

**Net assessment:** the reasoning for Must-Fix #1 is coherent for the SDK-requirement part, weak on why noindex+gating weren't at least partially applied, and the scope-deferral for the `?preview` case bypasses your own sign-off rather than securing it. Must-Fix #2 was addressed only implicitly, and the specific claim it leans on doesn't hold once you check `robots.txt` and the missing `Seo` usage. I wouldn't call these valid reasons to close — closer to a rationale for *why they chose not to fully fix it*, without actually getting the required agreement that that was okay.

---
name: project-pr42-env-security-gotcha
description: "GitHub Actions security gotcha found reviewing PR #42 (sync-env-vars-to-mrt): choice-type dropdown restrictions and repo-level secret inheritance can silently undermine an 'ungated target' fix"
metadata:
  type: project
---

While independently re-reviewing PR #42 (`feature/sync-env-vars-to-mrt` — on-demand workflow
to sync `.env.sample`-tagged GitHub Environment Variables to MRT), found a pattern worth
checking on any future workflow that uses a `workflow_dispatch` `type: choice` input as its
only restriction on which environment/target gets touched.

**The gotcha, in two parts:**
1. GitHub's own docs describe `choice` input validation only in terms of the Actions UI
   dropdown. They do not confirm (and I could not otherwise confirm) whether a `gh workflow
   run` / REST API dispatch with an arbitrary string for a `choice` input is rejected
   server-side, or silently accepted and passed through as a plain string. Treat this as
   unverified, not proven-safe, for any workflow where the choice list is meant to be a
   security boundary (e.g. "prod excluded from the dropdown").
2. Independent of (1): a job's `environment: ${{ inputs.target }}` only gives *that specific
   environment's own* secrets/protection-rules priority — it does **not** stop the job from
   also inheriting repo-level secrets of the same name. If `FOO_API_KEY` is set at the repo
   level (not per-environment), a job resolving to *any* environment string — including one
   never intended to be reachable, or one that doesn't even exist yet — still gets that
   credential. Removing a value from a `choice` list does not change this.

**Why it mattered here:** PR #42's original review found `prod` had an ungated path (empty
environment protection rules). The fix removed `prod` from the `target` choice list. On
independent re-check: `MRT_USER`/`MRT_API_KEY` (the credentials this workflow uses to write to
MRT) turned out to be **repo-level** secrets (`gh api repos/.../actions/secrets`), not
per-environment — so a bypassed dispatch to `prod` would still authenticate fine. The only
thing making this inert *today* is that `prod`'s GitHub Environment happens to have zero
Variables provisioned yet (`gh api repos/.../environments/prod/variables` → `total_count: 0`)
— a coincidence of current rollout state, not a designed safeguard, and it stops being true
the moment prod gets onboarded like `dev`/`test`/`sit`/`uat`/`staging` already are (7–16
variables each).

**How to apply:** for any workflow gating a destructive/sensitive target via `type: choice`
alone, check (a) whether the excluded value could still be reached via API/CLI dispatch, and
(b) `gh api repos/{repo}/actions/secrets` vs `gh api repos/{repo}/environments/{env}/secrets`
to see whether the credentials in play are actually scoped per-environment or repo-wide. If
repo-wide, the `choice` list is cosmetic, not a security boundary — recommend an explicit
allow-list check inside the script itself as defense-in-depth, independent of the YAML-level
restriction.

See [[user_role]] for the tier-1-approver / reviewer-identity context this review was done
under.

## PR #42 — Independent Deep-Dive Report

### Full history (reconstructed from timeline + all comments/reviews, not just the summary)

| When | Who | What |
|---|---|---|
| 07-24 02:17 | mani060689 | Opens PR, requests `tier-1-approvers` review |
| 07-24 02:21 | CodeRabbit | CHANGES_REQUESTED — invalid `variables: read` permission, missing MRT timeout, dead while-loop nitpick |
| 07-24 02:28–29 | mani060689 | Fixes all 3 in `c5ca8a1`, replies in-thread to each |
| 07-24 02:31 | mani060689 | Self-catches that `variables: read` isn't a real permission scope, swaps to `actions: read` in `cbbfb67` — **ahead of** CodeRabbit re-flagging it |
| 07-24 02:34 | CodeRabbit | Flags the (already-superseded) invalid permission as Critical; this review later gets dismissed |
| 07-24 02:39–03:39 | mani060689 | Pings `@coderabbitai please re review` / `review new changes` twice — both are no-ops (CodeRabbit's own reply says incremental auto-review was still active, so the explicit command did nothing extra). Meanwhile pushes `3f18a8c` (drops `GITHUB_TOKEN`+permission entirely, switches to a dedicated `GH_ENV_READ_TOKEN` PAT), `f0593ba`/`d6f08c0` (README docs) |
| 07-27 07:29 | marcelannavarro (you) | `@coderabbitai full-reivew` (typo — worked anyway) |
| 07-27 07:33 | CodeRabbit | CHANGES_REQUESTED — README should point to a fine-grained PAT, not classic |
| 07-27 12:28 | you | Full human review, CHANGES_REQUESTED: 2 must-fix (ungated prod path; CI secrets syncable to MRT) + 2 should-fix (PAT type; missing `URLError` handler) + 1 optional |
| 07-28 04:41 | mani060689 | Point-by-point reply claiming all 5 addressed in `d501409` |
| 07-28 04:41 | CodeRabbit | Auto-approves, 26 seconds later |
| 07-28 04:42 | mani060689 | Re-requests your review |
| 07-28 05:35 | you | Approved |

### Independent verification (I re-derived each of these myself against the live repo, not from CodeRabbit's or mani's say-so)

**Must-Fix #2 (CI secrets → MRT) — solidly confirmed, and proven against live data, not just code:**
I read the full `.env.sample` myself: every CI/tooling var is correctly untagged, every genuine runtime var is correctly tagged `mrt:true`. Then I went further and queried the **live** `dev` GitHub Environment's actual Variables — `CODERABBIT_API_KEY` and `CONFLUENCE_URL` are genuinely sitting there right now (expected, `scope:shared` pushes them everywhere via `switchEnv.mjs`). That's a real, present-tense proof point: the sync script's allow-list comes entirely from `.env.sample`'s tag, not from "whatever the environment happens to contain," so those two keys are structurally excluded regardless of what's upstream. I also confirmed `scripts/switchEnv.mjs` (Tier 2, untouched by this PR) tolerates the new `# mrt:true` line without breaking its own parser. One loose end, not a blocker: `PWA_KIT_SLAS_CLIENT_SECRET` is tagged `mrt:true` but is actually stored as a GitHub **Secret** (confirmed via `gh api .../actions/secrets`), not a Variable — and this workflow only ever reads the Variables endpoint. So that key will permanently show up as "skipped, not set" every run; the tag implies it's kept in sync, and it structurally can't be. Not a security issue — the opposite, a real secret correctly isn't sitting in plaintext — just worth a comment so nobody's confused later.

**Must-Fix #1 (ungated prod path) — real, but shallower than it looked; this is the one I'd push back on:**
`prod` is genuinely removed from the `workflow_dispatch` choice list. But I checked something neither CodeRabbit nor the original review re-verified after the fix landed: **is `type: choice` actually enforced server-side when dispatched via the REST API/`gh workflow run`, or only by the UI dropdown?** I checked GitHub's own docs directly — they describe UI behavior only and don't confirm either way. I can't prove this is bypassable, but I can't rule it out either, and that uncertainty matters here.

What I *can* prove, independently, from the live repo: **`MRT_USER`/`MRT_API_KEY` are repository-level secrets, not per-environment** (`gh api repos/.../actions/secrets`). That means they're inherited by *any* environment context a job resolves to — including a hypothetical bypassed `prod` dispatch. Nothing scopes them away from prod. The only reason this is inert *today* is that `prod`'s GitHub Environment currently has **zero Variables provisioned** (confirmed: `total_count: 0`, vs. 7–16 each for dev/test/sit/uat/staging) — so even a successful bypass would authenticate fine and find nothing to sync. That's a coincidence of current rollout state, not a designed safeguard, and it stops being true the day someone finishes onboarding prod like the other five tiers already are — which is presumably the whole point of this tool existing. **Recommend a one-line explicit allow-list check inside the Python script itself**, independent of the YAML `choice` restriction — costs nothing and removes any dependency on how GitHub actually handles this.

**Should-fix items — independently confirmed correct**, including one place mani's fix is better than it looks: keeping *both* `TimeoutError` and `URLError` handlers isn't redundant — Python's `urlopen` wraps a connect-phase timeout in `URLError`, but a response-read-phase timeout raises a bare `TimeoutError`. Both are needed to cover both phases.

**Things I checked that nobody else in this thread checked:**
- **Script-injection pattern**: all three Python steps pass every `${{ }}` expression through an `env:` block and read it via `os.environ[...]` — never spliced directly into the script text. This is the safe pattern throughout; nothing here is vulnerable to input-driven code execution.
- **The permission saga took two wrong attempts, not one.** `c5ca8a1`'s `variables: read` was invalid (CodeRabbit caught it). `cbbfb67`'s replacement, `actions: read`, was never flagged by CodeRabbit but is **also** wrong — `GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot read repo/environment Variables under any `permissions:` scope, confirmed via GitHub's REST API docs; that endpoint requires a real PAT or GitHub App token, full stop. Only the final swap to a dedicated `GH_ENV_READ_TOKEN` PAT (`3f18a8c`) actually works.
- **The PR's own test plan is 100% unchecked** (all 4 boxes), and I found out why: `GH_ENV_READ_TOKEN` doesn't exist as a secret anywhere in this repo yet — not at repo level, not in any of the six environments. As of right now, this workflow cannot succeed for *any* target, including the legitimate ones — it'll fail cleanly at the token-fetch step. Not a code defect, but this has never actually been run, dry or otherwise, across 8 commits and 3 review rounds.

### Bottom line

Nothing here can cause damage on merge — the feature is inert until someone creates `GH_ENV_READ_TOKEN`, and prod is unreachable in practice today regardless of the choice-bypass question. Must-Fix #2 is genuinely solid, proven against live data. Must-Fix #1 is real for the documented/intended usage path (the Actions UI) but is a single, UI-level control rather than defense-in-depth — I'd get the one-line target guard added before, or immediately after, merge, and definitely before prod gets real Variables provisioned. Two non-blocking fast-follows: actually run the dry-run test plan once `GH_ENV_READ_TOKEN` exists, and either drop the `mrt:true` tag from `PWA_KIT_SLAS_CLIENT_SECRET` or note that it won't actually sync via this path.

I'm not suggesting you walk back the approval — just flagging what's genuinely solid vs. what only *looks* solid. Want me to add the one-line guard now (Tier 1 file, but you're a confirmed tier-1-approver so I can proceed directly), or leave it as a fast-follow ticket?
